This is your own track, separate from your WGU degree. It has one destination: an OT threat/detection analyst or OT compliance role, and then the ICS security engineering path after that. Everything here is built for 5–7 hours a week in 15–30 minute pieces, because that is the time you actually have.

📘 DEFINITION

OT (Operational Technology): the computers that run physical things — pumps, valves, turbines, conveyor belts, chlorine dosing. If it can move something, heat something, or spill something, it is OT.

IT (Information Technology): the computers that run information — email, databases, the payroll system. Your current world.

ICS (Industrial Control System): the umbrella term for the control equipment inside OT. Used almost interchangeably with OT in job adverts.

The one deadline that actually matters

Before anything else, a date. I checked this against CompTIA's own site today, and it changes your first exam target:

★ ON THE EXAM

Security+ SY0-701 (the current version) retires around mid-May 2027. Its replacement, SY0-801, launches 17 November 2026 — about eight weeks from now.

My recommendation: sit SY0-701, and book it before May 2027. At 5–7 hours a week you will be ready around February 2027, comfortably inside the window. SY0-701 has three years of practice questions, videos and study guides behind it. SY0-801 will have almost none at launch, and you would be studying from material nobody has validated against the real exam yet. Being an early adopter costs you nothing here and buys you nothing.

How I will teach you

  1. One module at a time. I teach a module, quiz you at the end, and stop. When you say next, we move on. I will not dump six modules on you at once.
  2. Plain English first, then the technical detail. Every acronym gets defined the first time it appears — including the ones everyone assumes you know.
  3. Every lesson carries a real plant example. Abstract security concepts do not stick; a story about a chlorine pump does.
  4. I will tell you when you are not ready. If your quiz answers show a gap, I will say so plainly and we will go back. Encouragement that hides a problem is not kindness.
  5. Every exam fact is labelled. Green “verified” means I checked it against the vendor this week. Grey “not verified” means I could not reach the source and you should confirm it yourself before you rely on it.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The mistake almost everyone makes entering OT security is studying IT security and assuming it transfers. It transfers about 60% of the way. The other 40% is the part that gets you hired — and it is the part where the wrong answer is not a data breach, it is a chlorine release. That 40% is why this program exists and why Security+ is only step one.

You asked me to use your data background as a strength. It is a bigger one than you probably realise, and I want to be specific about why rather than just encouraging.

The thing OT security is actually short of

OT security has plenty of people who know plants and plenty who know IT security. What it is chronically short of is people who can look at a large volume of network data and tell what is normal. That is a data analysis problem wearing a hard hat.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Here is the thing that makes OT a gift to an analyst, and you should be able to say this sentence in an interview:

OT network traffic is boringly, beautifully predictable. An office network is chaos — people browse, stream, install things, work from cafes. A plant network does the same handful of things forever: this HMI polls that PLC for register 40001 every 500 milliseconds, all day, every day, for nine years.

That means baselining actually works in OT, where it barely works in IT. Anomaly detection in an office network drowns you in false positives. In a plant, a new source address or an unexpected function code is genuinely anomalous. Your SQL skills — group by, window functions, joins against an asset inventory — are the right tools for that job, not a transferable-skills consolation prize.

What maps directly

What you already doWhat it becomes in OT security
Writing SQL to profile a table — distinct values, counts, outliersBaselining a plant network: which devices talk to which, how often, using what function codes
GROUP BY + HAVING to find the odd rowsFinding the one engineering workstation that started writing to a PLC at 3am
Joining a fact table to a dimension tableJoining network flows to an asset inventory to spot traffic from a device that should not exist
Window functions over timeDetecting a polling interval that changed — often the first sign of a man-in-the-middle
Knowing when a dashboard is lying to youKnowing when a “normal” HMI screen is being fed replayed values — exactly what Stuxnet did
🏭 IN THE PLANT

The single most valuable OT detection skill is noticing that a value is too normal. Stuxnet recorded 21 seconds of legitimate sensor readings and replayed them to the operators' screens while it destroyed the centrifuges underneath. An operator saw a calm, steady process. A data analyst looking at the raw historian would have seen a signal with no noise in it — and real physical processes always have noise. That instinct is a data instinct, and you already have it.

How I will lean on this

Every course in this program has at least one lab built on your data skills rather than on tools you have never opened. The first is in the Labs chapter: pulling Modbus traffic out of a packet capture and using SQL to find the anomalous session. You will be doing familiar work on unfamiliar data — which is the fastest way into a new field.

Your time comes in three shapes. The mistake is treating them the same — trying to start a full lesson in a 15-minute gap, getting nowhere, and feeling like you are failing. You are not; you are using the wrong tool. Here is what each block is genuinely good for.

🕐 15 minutes — retrieval only

Never start new material in 15 minutes. Fifteen minutes is for pulling things back out of your head, which is what actually builds memory.

  • One flashcard deck review (the app's spaced-repetition queue)
  • 5–10 practice questions from a module you finished last week — not this week's
  • Read one case study callout and say out loud what the attacker did, from memory
  • Re-draw the Purdue Model on paper from memory. Ten seconds to draw, and it anchors half of GICSP.
★ ON THE EXAM

Retrieval practice beats re-reading by a wide margin in the research, and the gap widens the longer the delay before the test. Fifteen minutes of quizzing yourself is worth more than forty minutes of highlighting. This is why the short blocks are not the scraps of your study time — they are the engine of it.

🕐 30 minutes — one lesson, start to finish

This is the workhorse. Every lesson in this program is sized to fit a single 30-minute block: read it, work the examples, take the end-of-lesson quiz. One lesson, closed properly, beats two lessons half-read.

  1. 0–3 min: quiz yourself on the previous lesson first. Cold recall, no notes.
  2. 3–20 min: read the new lesson, plain-English part first. Write the key terms in your own words in the notebook — your words, not mine.
  3. 20–28 min: take the lesson quiz.
  4. 28–30 min: log your score in the tracker. Anything below 70% gets flagged as a weak area; we will come back to it.

🕐 90+ minutes — the weekend block, for labs only

Protect this. It is the only block long enough for hands-on work, and hands-on work is what gets you hired.

  • Build or extend a lab (OpenPLC, GRFICS, Wireshark, Zeek)
  • Write the lab up for your portfolio — the write-up is not optional, it is the deliverable
  • Take a full practice exam under timed conditions (end of each course only)
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The classic failure with 5–7 hours a week is spending all of it on new material because that feels like progress. You then arrive at the exam having seen everything once and retained about a third. Budget roughly 60% new material, 40% retrieval. The 15-minute blocks are where that 40% lives, which is why they matter more than their size suggests.

A realistic week

DayBlockWhat you do
Mon30 minNew lesson + quiz

Fri—Off. Planned, not skipped.
Sat90 minLab + write-up
Sun30 minNew lesson + weekly check-in with me

Total: 3 h 30 m of study + 90 min lab = 5 hours. That is the low end of your range on purpose, so a good week feels like a bonus instead of a week where you fell short.

You will miss weeks. A child gets sick, a deadline lands, you are simply too tired. The reason study plans fail is almost never the missed week — it is what the missed week does to your sense of whether you are still doing this. So the catch-up plan is written in advance, before you need it, when you are not feeling behind.

📘 DEFINITION

The rule: a missed week is a scheduled event, not a failure. You have four of them per year built into the roadmap already. Using one costs you nothing.

The 10-minute re-entry

Coming back is harder than keeping going, because you have to face how much you think you have forgotten. So the first session back is never new material. It is this, and it takes ten minutes:

  1. Do not re-read anything. Open the flashcard deck for the last module you finished and run it. You will get some wrong. That is the point — it shows you exactly where to aim.
  2. Look at your tracker and read the last line you wrote. Not the whole thing. One line.
  3. Do one lesson quiz you have taken before. Your score will have dropped a little. It comes back within two sessions.

That is it. You are back in. The next session is normal.

Scaling down without stopping

When you can see the week is going badly, drop tiers deliberately rather than just missing sessions:

TierTimeWhat you keep
Full5–7 h/wkEverything — lessons, labs, check-in
Reduced2–3 h/wkLessons + quizzes. Drop the lab; it moves to next week.
Maintenance~45 min/wkFlashcards only. Three 15-minute reviews. No new material at all.
Pause0Declared, with a return date. Tell me the date and I will hold the plan.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Maintenance tier is the one that saves the program. Forty-five minutes of flashcards a week holds nearly everything you have learned in place. Zero minutes a week for a month costs you roughly three weeks of re-learning. When you are drowning, do not choose between full effort and nothing — choose maintenance.

What it costs the roadmap

Nothing dramatic, and I want you to see the numbers so a bad month does not feel fatal:

  • One week at maintenance instead of full: pushes your exam date by about 4 days
  • A four-week pause: pushes it by about a month
  • Security+ has a 13-week buffer before SY0-701 retires. You can lose three months and still make it.

Tell me when a week goes wrong and I will re-cut the dates rather than leaving you to feel behind against a schedule that no longer reflects your life.

2. The weak-area log — the one that matters most

This is the highest-value document in the whole program. Every question you get wrong goes in it, in your own words, in this shape:

TopicWhat I got wrongThe actual rule

Before every exam, the last thing you read is this log — not your notes, not a textbook. It is a list of the exact mistakes you personally are prone to, which is worth more per minute than any revision guide ever written.

3. Next-review dates — let the app do it

Do not hand-schedule reviews. Use the flashcard queue, which already spaces them. The only thing you schedule by hand is the end-of-course full practice exam, which goes in the planner two weeks before your target exam date — never the week before, because you need time to act on what it tells you.

The weekly check-in — what to send me

Once a week, in four lines. That is genuinely all I need to re-plan:

📮 PASTE THIS TO ME

From that I will: adjust your target dates if needed, pick your next module, and build a targeted mini-quiz on the exact topics you missed. ⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Flashcards are where the 15-minute blocks pay off. Two ways to use them: the app's own flashcard screen, or Anki if you want them on your phone during a commute.

📘 DEFINITION

Spaced repetition: reviewing a fact at increasing intervals — a day, then three days, then a week, then a month. Each successful recall pushes the next review further out, so your limited time concentrates on what you are about to forget.

Anki: the standard free spaced-repetition app (desktop, Android free; iOS paid). It imports plain text files.

The import format

Every flashcard set in this program is written as a tab-separated front → back file, which Anki imports directly with no configuration:

📄 ot-ics-m1.txt
What does the C in the CIA triad stand for, and what does it mean?	Confidentiality — only those authorised can read the data
In OT, which letter of the CIA triad usually comes FIRST, and why?	Availability — a control system that stops responding can cause a physical incident; a plant that cannot be controlled is dangerous
What is a compensating control?	A different control used when the intended one is not feasible, giving comparable protection

One tab between front and back, one card per line. In Anki: File → Import → choose the file → Field separator: Tab → Import.

📥 Download the first deck (54 cards)

Covers Security+ Module 1, the exam facts from the roadmap, OT foundations, the safety module and all six case studies. A new deck arrives with each module.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

If you paste these into a spreadsheet first, make sure it does not convert the tab into multiple spaces — Anki will then import the whole line as the front of the card with an empty back. Import the .txt directly.

Three rules for cards that actually work

  1. One fact per card. A card asking “list the five Security+ domains” is five cards pretending to be one, and you will keep failing it and feel stupid.
  2. Write the back in your own words wherever you can. A card in my phrasing tests whether you can recognise my phrasing. A card in yours tests whether you understand it.
  3. Make cards ask questions, not show terms. “Modbus” → definition is a weak card. “Which industrial protocol has no authentication at all, so any device on the network can command a PLC?” → “Modbus” is a strong one, because that is the shape the exam and the job both use.
★ ON THE EXAM

Special case — GICSP is open book. For that exam your flashcards do double duty: they become the index you carry in. Start building it from the first GICSP module, not the month before. We will cover how to structure it when we get there, but know now that nothing you write for GICSP is throwaway.

Certificates get you past the filter. The portfolio gets you the interview, and then it gives you something to actually talk about for forty-five minutes. For someone moving into OT without plant experience, it is the single strongest thing you can build.

The repository

One public GitHub repository, ot-security-labs. One folder per lab. A README at the top that is a table, not prose — hiring managers scan, they do not read.

📄 README.md
# OT / ICS Security Labs

Hands-on labs built while working toward Security+, ISA/IEC 62443 CFS,
GICSP and GRID. Every lab uses free, open tools.

| # | Lab | Skills demonstrated | Tools |
|---|-----|---------------------|-------|
| 01 | Building an ICS test bench | Virtualisation, network segmentation | OpenPLC, VirtualBox |
| 02 | Reading Modbus off the wire | Protocol analysis, OT traffic literacy | Wireshark |

The write-up template

Use this for every lab. It is deliberately short — a lab you write up in 25 minutes is a lab you will actually write up.

📄 lab-NN/README.md
# Lab NN — [Title]

**Date:** 2026-10-04
**Time spent:** 90 min
**Maps to:** GICSP objective — ICS protocols; Security+ 4.1 — monitoring

## The question
One sentence. What was I trying to find out or prove?

## Setup
What I built, with enough detail that someone could rebuild it.
Include the network diagram (hand-drawn photo is fine).

## What I did
Numbered steps. Commands in code blocks. Screenshots of the
interesting moments, not of every screen.

## What I found
The actual result. Include the output.

## What surprised me
The most valuable section. Interviewers read this one.
What did not work the way I expected, and why?

## What an attacker could do with this
One paragraph. Connects the lab to real risk.

## Safety / environmental note
If this were a real plant: what physical harm could result,
and what safety system should independently prevent it?
🏭 IN THE PLANT

That last section is the one that will separate you from every other candidate. Most people writing ICS labs stop at “I sent a Modbus write and the coil changed.” If you add “in a real plant this coil is a pump start, and here is why the Safety Instrumented System must stop it independently of the PLC” — you are demonstrating that you think like an OT engineer, not an IT person with a new hobby. That is precisely the gap employers are hiring to fill.

Course one of five. Security+ is a general IT security certification — it is not about OT at all. You are taking it because it is the credential that gets your application read, and because the vocabulary it teaches is the vocabulary every later course assumes you already have.

✅ VERIFIED

Exam format — verified against CompTIA, 24 Sept 2026

  • Code: SY0-701
  • Questions: maximum 90, mixed multiple-choice and performance-based (PBQs)
  • Time: 90 minutes
  • Passing score: 750 out of 100–900
  • Retires: around mid-May 2027 (successor SY0-801 launches 17 Nov 2026)

The five domains, and where your time should go

#DomainWeightYour effort
1.0General Security Concepts12%Light — mostly vocabulary
2.0Threats, Vulnerabilities & Mitigations22%Heavy
3.0Security Architecture18%Medium — your networking gaps live here
4.0Security Operations28%Heaviest — and your strongest
5.0Security Program Management & Oversight20%Medium — dry, but directly relevant to OT compliance roles
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Domain 4 is 28% of the exam and it is monitoring, logging, alerting and incident response. That is the closest thing on this exam to work you already do. Expect it to be your best domain, and do not let that make you complacent about Domain 3, where subnetting and firewall rules will bite you if your networking is thin.

Total study time and the schedule

~100 hours over 18 weeks at 5–6 hours a week. That is slightly more than the usual estimate, because I am deliberately building extra depth in Domains 3 and 4 — those carry into GICSP and GRID, so hours spent there are spent twice.

WeeksFocusMilestone
1–2Domain 1 — concepts & vocabularyLab 01: build the test bench
3–6Domain 2 — threats & vulnerabilitiesCase study: Stuxnet
7–10Domain 3 — architecture (+ networking foundations)Lab 02: Modbus on the wire
11–14Domain 4 — operations, monitoring, IRLab 03: SQL baselining
15–16Domain 5 — governance, risk, complianceEnvironmental & safety module

Exam-day strategy and the traps for this exam specifically

  1. PBQs come first and they eat clock. Performance-based questions are usually at the start. If one is fighting you, flag it and move on — you can return. The classic failure is spending 25 of your 90 minutes on two PBQs and then rushing 80 multiple-choice questions.
  2. “BEST” and “MOST likely” mean several answers are correct. CompTIA writes questions where two or three options are genuinely true and one is most true. If two answers look right, you have understood the question, not misread it — now pick on scope.
  3. Answer as a policy-following employee, not as a technical expert. If an option says “escalate to management” or “follow the incident response plan”, that is very often the intended answer even when a clever technical fix exists.
  4. 750/900 is not 83%. It is a scaled score; questions are not weighted equally and the raw percentage needed is lower. Do not panic-estimate mid-exam.
  5. Do not study SY0-801 material. Until you have passed, ignore anything labelled V8. Mixing objective sets is how people fail.
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The OT trap in reverse: Security+ answers are written for office IT. When a question asks about patching, the right Security+ answer is “patch promptly.” In OT that answer can be dangerously wrong — you cannot reboot a turbine controller on Patch Tuesday. Answer Security+ questions the IT way. I will flag every place where the OT answer differs, because those flags are exactly what GICSP tests later.

Maps to SY0-701 objectives 1.1 (compare and contrast various types of security controls) and 1.2 (summarize fundamental security concepts). About 30 minutes.

Plain English first

Security has exactly three goals. Everything else in this certification is machinery for achieving one of them.

  1. Keep secrets secret. Only the right people can read the thing.
  2. Keep the truth true. Nobody changed the thing without permission.
  3. Keep it working. The thing is there when you need it.

Those three are called the CIA triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. Nothing to do with the intelligence agency.

And a security control is just a thing you put in place to protect something. A lock. A password rule. A camera. A policy document. A guard. The exam cares less about what controls are than about how you classify them — and it classifies them two different ways at once, which is the single biggest source of lost marks in this domain.

The technical detail

📘 DEFINITION

Confidentiality: information is available only to those authorised. Achieved by encryption, access control, data classification.

Integrity: information has not been altered by anyone unauthorised, and you can prove it. Achieved by hashing, digital signatures, checksums.

Availability: the system is accessible when needed. Achieved by redundancy, backups, failover, capacity planning.

Non-repudiation: the sender cannot later deny having sent it. Achieved by digital signatures and audit logging. Related to integrity but a separate concept — the exam tests this distinction.

Axis 1 — control categories (what kind of thing it is)

CategoryWhat it isExamples
TechnicalImplemented by technologyFirewall, encryption, antivirus, MFA
ManagerialAdministrative — how risk is governedRisk assessments, security policy, vendor reviews
OperationalCarried out by people, day to daySecurity awareness training, guards, change management
PhysicalAffects the physical worldFences, locks, badge readers, bollards, lighting

Axis 2 — control types (what the thing does)

TypeWhat it doesExamples
PreventiveStops it happeningFirewall rule, door lock, MFA
DeterrentDiscourages the attemptWarning sign, visible camera, "prosecution will follow" banner
DetectiveNotices it happenedIDS, log review, motion sensor, audit
CorrectiveFixes it afterwardsRestore from backup, patch, incident response
CompensatingStands in when the intended control is not feasibleExtra monitoring on a server that cannot be patched
DirectiveTells people what to doAcceptable use policy, posted procedure
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The mistake that costs people marks: treating these as one list. They are two independent axes, and every control has a value on both.

A security guard is physical (category) and simultaneously deterrent, preventive and detective (type). A camera is physical and both deterrent and detective. Read the question to see which axis it wants. “Which category?” wants technical/managerial/operational/physical. “Which type?” wants preventive/deterrent/detective/corrective/compensating/directive.

🏭 The real-world OT example

🏭 IN THE PLANT

A water treatment plant doses chlorine into drinking water. Too little and pathogens survive; too much and you injure the people drinking it. The dosing setpoint lives in a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) — a ruggedised industrial computer that reads sensors and drives pumps and valves.

Now place the controls:

  • Technical / preventive: a firewall permitting only the operator workstation to reach the PLC
  • Technical / detective: an alert when the chlorine setpoint changes outside a maintenance window
  • Physical / preventive: the PLC cabinet is locked and the key is controlled
  • Operational / directive: a written procedure requiring two-person sign-off for setpoint changes
  • Managerial: the annual risk assessment that decided all of the above

And the one that is not a cyber control at all: a mechanical relief mechanism sized so the dosing pump physically cannot deliver a dangerous concentration, whatever the PLC is told to do. That is engineered safety, and it is the layer that holds when every cyber control has failed.

🦺 SAFETY & ENVIRONMENT

Now the CIA triad in a plant, and why OT people re-order it.

In your current job, a database going offline for an hour is an inconvenience. In a plant, a control system going unresponsive for an hour can mean a tank overflows into a river. So OT conventionally prioritises Availability first, then Integrity, then Confidentiality — the reverse of IT. Nobody is much troubled if a competitor learns the pump's speed; everybody is troubled if the pump stops answering.

Integrity deserves a second look though, because OT's worst incidents are integrity failures dressed as normality: a sensor reporting a tank is half full when it is overflowing. The system is perfectly available. It is lying.

Defence in depthMultiple independent layers, so one failure is not total failure
Zero TrustNever trust by network location; verify every request explicitly
PLCProgrammable Logic Controller — the industrial computer that drives physical equipment

★ ON THE EXAM

Zero Trust in SY0-701 has named parts, and they are examinable. The Control Plane makes decisions (Policy Engine, Policy Administrator, Policy Decision Point, adaptive identity, threat scope reduction). The Data Plane carries them out (Policy Enforcement Point, the subject/system, the implicit trust zone). If a question names “Policy Enforcement Point”, it is asking about the Data Plane.

This is the module that makes you an OT security professional rather than an IT security professional who has read an ICS book. It is also the part most courses skip.

Plain English first

In IT security, the worst case is that data is stolen, destroyed or held to ransom. Serious, expensive, sometimes ruinous — but it is information harm.

In OT, the worst case is that something physical happens that hurts people or the environment. A tank overflows. A pipeline over-pressurises. Untreated sewage reaches a river. Chlorine gas escapes. A turbine tears itself apart.

That difference changes the entire discipline. It changes what you protect first, what risk means, who you answer to, and what counts as success.

🦺 SAFETY & ENVIRONMENT

The sentence to internalise: in OT, cybersecurity is a safety discipline that happens to use computers. The reason a water utility employs security people is not to protect data. It is to make sure the water stays drinkable. Say that in an interview and you will sound like someone who belongs there.

Process safety — the discipline that was already there

Long before anyone worried about hacking a plant, engineers had a mature discipline for keeping dangerous processes from harming people. You are joining that discipline, not replacing it.

📘 DEFINITION

Process safety: preventing the unintentional release of energy or hazardous material from an industrial process.

HAZOP (Hazard and Operability study): a structured workshop that walks through a process asking “what if this goes wrong?” for every part of it.

Layers of Protection Analysis (LOPA): counting the independent protective layers between a hazard and a consequence, and checking there are enough.

Independent Protection Layer (IPL): a safeguard that works even if the others have failed. The word that matters is independent.

The onion: layers of protection

Picture the hazard at the centre. Each ring must fail before the next is tested:

RingLayerWho owns it
1Process design (make it inherently safer)Process engineers
2Basic Process Control System (BPCS) — the normal PLC/DCS controlControl engineers
3Alarms and operator interventionOperations
4Safety Instrumented System (SIS) — independent shutdownSafety engineers
5Physical relief — relief valves, rupture discs, bundsMechanical, no software at all
6Emergency response, evacuation, containmentEveryone
⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Here is the insight the whole module turns on. A cyberattack is uniquely dangerous to this model because it can attack several rings at once. Natural failures are independent — a stuck valve does not also blind the alarm. An attacker with access to the control network can change the setpoint (ring 2), suppress the alarm (ring 3), and feed the operator a normal-looking screen. Independence is the assumption the whole safety case rests on, and cyber is the one hazard that breaks it deliberately. This is exactly why the SIS must be genuinely separate — and exactly what TRITON attacked.

How cyber becomes environmental harm

A real one, and it needed no attacker. In Maroochy Shire, Queensland, Australia (2000), a rejected contractor used insider knowledge and radio equipment to issue commands to sewage pumping stations. You asked for TRITON in depth. To understand why it is the most frightening ICS attack yet seen, you first need to understand what it attacked — so we build the Safety Instrumented System first, then break it.

Plain English first

Every dangerous industrial process has two separate control systems, and the separation is the whole point.

  1. The control system runs the process day to day. It holds the reactor at 300°C, keeps the tank at 60% full, runs the pumps. It is trying to make the plant work.
  2. The safety system does nothing at all, almost all the time. It watches, and if things go badly wrong it shuts the process down safely. It is trying to make the plant not kill anyone.

They are separate on purpose. If the control system fails — or is compromised — the safety system is supposed to be untouched and still able to stop the process. It is the last automated line before physical relief valves and emergency response.

📘 DEFINITION

SIS (Safety Instrumented System): an independent system of sensors, logic solver and final elements that takes a process to a safe state when defined limits are exceeded.

SIF (Safety Instrumented Function): one specific protective action, e.g. “if pressure exceeds 12 bar, close valve XV-101.”

Logic solver: the safety-rated controller that decides — the SIS equivalent of a PLC. Triconex is a well-known family.

SIL (Safety Integrity Level) 1–4: how reliable a SIF must be. Higher SIL = lower permitted probability of failure on demand. SIL 3 is common for serious hazards; SIL 4 is rare and very expensive.

IEC 61511 / ISA 84: the standard governing SIS for the process industries — essentially the same document, ISA 84 being the US adoption. IEC 61508 is the parent standard for the equipment itself.

The technical detail: why an SIS is different

PropertyBasic control system (BPCS)Safety system (SIS)
JobKeep the process running wellTake the process to a safe state
Normal stateConstantly actingDoing nothing, watching
Failure modeFails in whatever directionFails safe — loss of signal trips the process
Change controlRoutine engineering changeFormal, documented, often requires a physical key switch
CertificationNone requiredCertified to a SIL under IEC 61508/61511
Independence—Must be independent of the BPCS — separate sensors, separate logic, separate final elements
★ ON THE EXAM

The key-switch detail is examinable and it is the hinge of the TRITON story. Triconex controllers have a physical mode switch with positions including RUN, PROGRAM and REMOTE. In RUN, the logic cannot be changed over the network. Changing safety logic is supposed to require someone to physically walk to the cabinet and turn a key. That is a deliberately analogue defence against exactly this attack.

TRITON / TRISIS / HatMan — what actually happened

Three names for the same malware: TRITON (FireEye), TRISIS (Dragos), HatMan (US CISA/ICS-CERT). All the same thing.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

From memory, not verified this session. The account below reflects the widely-published analyses. The narrative is well corroborated across vendors and government reporting, but I could not re-check specifics today.

  1. Target: a petrochemical facility in Saudi Arabia, discovered 2017.
  2. Entry and traversal: the attackers got into the IT network, then crossed to the OT network, and eventually reached an engineering workstation used to program the Triconex safety controllers. Note that they did not attack the SIS from the internet — they attacked the computer that is allowed to talk to it. That is the pattern.
  3. The opening they used: the key switch on the target controller had reportedly been left in PROGRAM rather than RUN. The analogue defence was there and was not engaged.
  4. What the malware did: it implanted a backdoor into the safety controller's firmware, giving the attackers the ability to read and write the safety logic at will — in effect, the power to decide whether the plant's last automated protection would function.
  5. How it was found: the attackers made a mistake. Their code did not match what the controller expected, and the Triconex failed safe and tripped the plant. Twice. The operator investigated an unexplained shutdown and found the malware.
🦺 SAFETY & ENVIRONMENT

Why this is the line-crossing attack. Stuxnet destroyed machines. Ukraine turned off the lights. TRITON is the first known malware built to disable the system whose only job is to stop people dying.

Think about what that means as a plan. Compromising an SIS alone causes nothing — the safety system does nothing when the process is behaving. It only has value to an attacker in combination with a second attack on the process itself: you neutralise the protection, then you cause the over-pressure. The intended outcome of that combination is an explosion or toxic release, with the safeguards intentionally disabled.

The plant was saved by the attackers' bug and by a controller that failed safe as designed. That is not a security control. That is luck plus good engineering.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The lesson people take from TRITON is usually the wrong one. It is not “patch your Triconex.” It is that the independence of your safety layer is a claim that must be defended, not assumed. If the same engineering workstation, the same domain credentials, the same network and the same technician reach both the BPCS and the SIS, then your Layers of Protection Analysis is counting layers that are not actually independent — and the safety case built on it is overstating your protection.

What you would actually do about it

  1. Key switch in RUN. Auditable, and check it physically. The cheapest control here is a procedure and a walk.
  2. Separate the SIS network from the BPCS network — its own zone, its own conduit, in 62443 terms.
  3. A dedicated safety engineering workstation that does not also program the BPCS, does not browse the web, and does not share credentials.
  4. Monitor for safety-system programming traffic. This is a detection problem, and it is a beautiful one for you: programming an SIS is a rare, scheduled event. Any such traffic outside a maintenance window is high-signal, low-noise alerting — the opposite of typical IT alerting.
  5. Include cyber in the HAZOP. Ask explicitly: which of these protection layers could a single attacker defeat together?
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Your portfolio lab for this module: build a detection rule that alerts on any write or programming-mode traffic to a safety controller outside an approved change window, joined against a change-management table. In SQL terms that is a left join from network events to an approved-changes table, keeping the rows where the change record is null. It is a fifteen-line query, it is genuinely how this is done in practice, and you can explain it in an interview in ninety seconds.

Five incidents come up in GICSP, in GRID, and in every OT interview. Learn them as patterns, not anecdotes — what the attacker needed, what failed, what would have caught it.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

From memory, not verified this session for the technical details of each incident, with one exception I checked today and flag below. These accounts are well corroborated in public reporting, but confirm specifics before citing them professionally.

1. Stuxnet (discovered 2010) — the integrity attack

  • Target: uranium enrichment centrifuges, Natanz, Iran.
  • Route in: removable media across an air gap. The air gap was real and it did not help.
  • What it did: altered PLC logic to vary centrifuge speeds destructively, while replaying recorded normal sensor data to the operator displays.
  • Pattern to learn: the operator's screen is not ground truth. A compromised control system can lie fluently. This is why OT monitoring watches the network and the physics, not just the HMI.
📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

Your angle: replayed data has a statistical signature. Real process data has noise, drift and correlation with other variables. A replayed loop is too clean and eventually repeats. Detecting that is a time-series problem, and it is exactly the sort of thing a data analyst notices and a control engineer does not.

2. Ukraine grid, December 2015 — the hands-on-keyboard attack

  • Result: roughly 225,000 customers lost power.
  • Route in: spear-phishing into the IT network, credential theft, then legitimate remote access into the control network.
  • What they did: human operators manually clicked breakers open through the utility's own HMI software. They also wiped workstations, corrupted serial-to-Ethernet converter firmware so breakers could not be reclosed remotely, and ran a telephone denial-of-service against the call centre so customers could not report outages.
  • Recovery: engineers drove to substations and closed breakers by hand. Manual fallback saved them.
  • Pattern to learn: no ICS-specific malware was needed. Stolen credentials plus the utility's own tools were enough. Remote access is the front door of OT.

3. Ukraine grid, December 2016 — CRASHOVERRIDE / Industroyer

  • The leap: 2015 was people clicking. 2016 was automated malware that spoke the grid protocols natively — IEC 60870-5-101/104, IEC 61850, OPC DA.
  • Why it matters: it was modular and re-targetable. Swap the protocol module and point it at another utility. That is a weapons platform, not a one-off tool.
  • Pattern to learn: protocol-aware malware makes attacks scale. This is the strongest argument for protocol-aware monitoring — you cannot spot a malicious IEC 104 command with a firewall that only sees ports.

4. TRITON / TRISIS (2017) — the safety attack

Covered in depth in the Environmental & Safety module. The one-line version: the first known malware built to disable a Safety Instrumented System, foiled by the attackers' own bug and a controller that failed safe.

5. Colonial Pipeline (May 2021) — the one that was not an OT attack

  • What happened: DarkSide ransomware hit the IT network. Reported initial access was a legacy VPN account without multi-factor authentication.
  • Critical detail: the OT systems were not compromised. The company shut the pipeline down itself — reportedly because the billing system was down and they could not measure what they were delivering, and out of caution about IT/OT separation.
  • Result: fuel shortages across the US East Coast, panic buying, emergency declarations. Then the TSA Security Directives, which made pipeline cyber requirements mandatory.
  • Pattern to learn: an IT incident can stop a physical process without ever touching OT. If you cannot bill, measure or schedule, you may not be able to operate. Business-process dependency is an OT risk, and people miss it constantly.
★ ON THE EXAM

Colonial is the standard exam trap in this set. A question describing it and asking “which OT systems were compromised?” is testing whether you know the answer is none. It is also the standard interview question, for the same reason.

6. Oldsmar, Florida (February 2021) — and why I am teaching it differently

✅ VERIFIED

Verified 24 September 2026. This is the one I checked, because it is almost universally taught wrong.

The story as told in 2021: an intruder accessed the water treatment plant's HMI remotely and raised the sodium hydroxide (lye) setpoint from about 100 parts per million to 11,100 ppm — a poisoning attempt. An alert operator saw the cursor move, reverted it, and was hailed as a hero. It launched a federal advisory and a thousand conference talks.

What actually came out later: the FBI investigated for months and could not confirm any intrusion. Officials including the former city manager subsequently said it was most likely employee error — plausibly the same operator — and characterised it as a non-event.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Why I am keeping it in the syllabus anyway, with the correction: because the corrected version teaches you more than the myth did, and it teaches the thing your target job is actually made of.

  • Attribution discipline. “A value changed unexpectedly” is not “we were attacked.” A detection analyst who cannot hold that distinction will burn their credibility inside a year.
  • Anomaly ≠ adversary. Most OT anomalies are misconfiguration, maintenance, or a tired human. Your job is to find the ones that are not, and to say honestly which is which.
  • The underlying risk was still real. Shared remote-access credentials, unsupported operating systems and no alerting on setpoint changes were genuinely present in that sector. The vulnerability was real even though the attack was not.

If an interviewer raises Oldsmar as an attack, saying “actually the FBI could not confirm an intrusion and it was likely operator error — but the exposure it revealed was real” will do more for you than any certificate on your CV.

Everything here is free. You need a laptop with virtualisation and about 8 GB of RAM — 16 GB is comfortable. Budget one 90-minute weekend block; do not attempt this in 30 minutes.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Rule zero: everything in this lab runs on an isolated host-only virtual network. Never point these tools at equipment you do not own. Scanning a real control system can crash it — PLCs have been knocked over by an ordinary port scan, because they were never built to expect one. “I was only scanning” is not a defence, and in OT it can be a safety incident.

The tools, and what each is for

ToolCostWhat it gives you
VirtualBoxFreeThe virtual machines everything else runs in
OpenPLCFreeA real, standards-based soft PLC. Runs actual ladder logic and speaks Modbus TCP.
WiresharkFreePacket capture and analysis. Decodes Modbus natively.
GRFICSFreeA simulated chemical plant with a 3D process view — you can watch your attack cause a physical consequence
ZeekFreeTurns packet captures into structured logs. This is your bridge — it produces tables.
Security OnionFreeA full monitoring stack. Heavier; save it for later labs.
ConpotFreeAn ICS honeypot — pretends to be a PLC and logs who talks to it

Step by step

  1. Install VirtualBox from virtualbox.org.
  2. Create a host-only network. VirtualBox → Tools → Network → Host-only Networks → Create. Note the subnet it gives you (commonly 192.168.56.0/24). Do not attach these VMs to a bridged adapter.
  3. Build the PLC VM. Install Ubuntu Server (minimal is fine), attach it to the host-only network, then install OpenPLC following the project's instructions. Web interface on port 8080; Modbus TCP on port 502.
  4. Write one piece of ladder logic. The simplest useful program: a coil that turns on when a holding register exceeds a threshold. In plant terms: “if tank level > 80%, start the discharge pump.”
  5. Build the workstation VM. Ubuntu Desktop or Kali, same host-only network. Install Wireshark and a Modbus client (mbpoll or a Python script using pymodbus).
  6. Prove the loop works. From the workstation, read the register. Write a value above the threshold. Watch the coil change. You have just commanded a PLC.
  7. Capture it. Run Wireshark on the workstation, filter on modbus, and repeat step 6. Save the capture as lab01.pcap — the next lab uses it.
🏭 IN THE PLANT

Pause on step 6, because it is the moment the field makes sense. You issued a write. There was no login, no password, no certificate, no question of who you were. Modbus has no authentication whatsoever — it was designed in 1979 for a serial cable inside a locked cabinet, where being physically present was the authentication. Everything else in OT security is a response to that sentence.

Your write-up

Use the portfolio template. For “what surprised me”, the honest answer is usually step 6. For the safety note: if that coil were a real discharge pump on a wastewater holding tank, an unauthenticated write would be an unpermitted discharge under the Clean Water Act — and the independent protection layer would be a high-level float switch wired directly to a pump interlock, not to the PLC.

This is your lab. Everything so far has been learning someone else's tools; this one is you doing what you already do well, on data that happens to come from a plant.

📊 YOUR DATA EDGE

The premise: OT traffic is repetitive to a degree office traffic never is. An HMI polls a PLC every 500 ms, using the same function codes, for the same registers, for years. That means a baseline is genuinely achievable — and once you have one, anomalies are obvious rather than buried. This is why baselining works in OT and barely works in IT, and it is the single most marketable thing in this whole program for you.

Step 1 — get traffic worth analysing

Leave the Lab 01 rig running for 20–30 minutes with a script polling the PLC on a fixed interval, so you have a realistic baseline. Then, in the last two minutes, do three “suspicious” things from a second workstation VM:

  • read a register range nobody normally reads
  • issue a write (function code 6 or 16) from a host that only ever reads
  • poll at a noticeably different interval

Step 2 — turn packets into rows

This is the step that converts a security problem into a data problem:

zeek -r lab02.pcap
# produces conn.log, modbus.log and others

# Zeek logs are tab-separated with a header block.
# Strip the headers and load into SQLite:
cat modbus.log | grep -v '^#' > modbus.tsv
sqlite3 ot.db
.mode tabs
.import modbus.tsv modbus_raw

Now you have a table. You are home.

Step 3 — the queries

Four queries. Each one corresponds to a real detection used in production OT monitoring.

a) Who talks to whom? (the asset relationship baseline)

SELECT src_ip, dst_ip, COUNT(*) AS msgs,
       MIN(ts) AS first_seen, MAX(ts) AS last_seen
FROM   modbus_raw
GROUP  BY src_ip, dst_ip
ORDER  BY msgs DESC;

A plant network has a short list here. A new pair appearing is one of the highest-value alerts in all of OT security.

b) Who writes, and did they ever write before?

SELECT src_ip,
       SUM(CASE WHEN func LIKE '%READ%'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reads,
       SUM(CASE WHEN func LIKE '%WRITE%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS writes
FROM   modbus_raw
GROUP  BY src_ip
HAVING writes > 0;

Most hosts should have zero writes. An HMI writes; a historian never should. A host whose write count goes from 0 to 1 is the whole ballgame.

c) Did the polling rhythm change? (the window function)

WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT src_ip, ts,
         ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY src_ip ORDER BY ts) AS gap
  FROM   modbus_raw
)
SELECT src_ip,
       ROUND(AVG(gap),3)  AS avg_gap,
       ROUND(MIN(gap),3)  AS min_gap,
       ROUND(MAX(gap),3)  AS max_gap,
       COUNT(*)           AS samples
FROM   gaps
WHERE  gap IS NOT NULL
GROUP  BY src_ip;

A legitimate poller has a tiny spread between min and max. A wide spread, or a sudden change in the average, suggests something else is generating the traffic.

d) The one that matters most — writes outside a change window

CREATE TABLE approved_changes (
  host TEXT, window_start REAL, window_end REAL, ticket TEXT
);

SELECT m.ts, m.src_ip, m.dst_ip, m.func
FROM   modbus_raw m
LEFT   JOIN approved_changes c
       ON  m.src_ip = c.host
       AND m.ts BETWEEN c.window_start AND c.window_end
WHERE  m.func LIKE '%WRITE%'
  AND  c.ticket IS NULL;
🏭 IN THE PLANT

That last query is a left join keeping the unmatched rows — the first anti-join you ever learned. In a plant it means: every command that changed something, with no approved change record behind it. Commercial OT security platforms sell this as a headline feature. You just wrote it in eight lines, and you understand exactly what it does and where it would produce false positives. That understanding is what they are hiring.

Step 4 — write it up honestly

In “what surprised me”, address the thing a good interviewer will probe: how many false positives did these produce, and what would you do about them? The answer for query (d) is usually “a lot, until the change-management data is trustworthy” — and noticing that detection quality is downstream of data quality is a genuinely senior observation.

🦺 SAFETY & ENVIRONMENT

Safety note for the write-up: a Modbus write to a coil in this lab is a bit flipping. In a wastewater plant it is a pump starting. Your detection query is one layer; it does not stop anything. The layer that stops it is the interlock wired independently of the PLC. Say so in your write-up — it shows you know the difference between detecting and preventing, which is the difference between a monitoring analyst and an engineer.

The template lives in the Study Systems chapter — this section is the standards that make a write-up worth reading, plus the sequence of labs ahead so you can see where this goes.

Five rules

  1. Write it the same day. A lab written up a week later loses every detail worth having, especially the things that went wrong.
  2. Include what failed. “OpenPLC would not start until I realised the host-only adapter was on the wrong subnet” is more convincing than a flawless account. Real engineers recognise real debugging.
  3. One diagram per lab. Hand-drawn and photographed is completely fine — arguably better, because it is obviously yours.
  4. Never publish anything from a real system. No employer IPs, no real captures, no screenshots from work. Lab data only. Getting this wrong ends careers in this field.
  5. Close every write-up with the safety paragraph. It is what separates your repository from the hundreds of identical “I ran Wireshark” repositories.
